newsitem.title: USA: TWA seeks dismissal of Flight 800 suits.
newsitem.headline: TWA seeks dismissal of Flight 800 suits.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent

TWA has sought the dismissal of lawsuits blaming it for an explosion aboard Flight 800 as the cause of the tragedy has not been determined and could still be linked to anything from a missile to a meteorite, one of its lawyers said on Wednesday.
The Paris-bound Boeing 747 exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean on July 17, just minutes after taking off from Kennedy International Airport. All 230 passengers and crew on board were killed.

More than 20 suits have been filed against Trans World Airlines and Boeing Co. maker of the jet, alleging the explosion was caused by a mechanical malfunction. The suits, filed in federal courts in Manhattan and Brooklyn, also asked that the defendants be held liable if it was found the explosion was caused by a bomb.
"From our point of view, the suits are premature in that nobody has identified any cause," Randal Craft, a lawyer with TWA's outside counsel Haight, Gardner, Poor & Havens said on Wednesday.

TWA's response to the lawsuits was filed last week in federal courts located in the Southern and Eastern Districts of New York. It listed 22 possible defences to the suits and said the appropriate defences could be argued after a cause was determined.
The document said TWA had fully answered the allegations in the lawsuits and requested the dismissal of the complaints.
Craft said the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation was scheduled to meet on Jan. 24 to discuss where the cases would be consolidated.

The National Transportation Safety Board said last month that a buildup of volatile vapours in the 747's partially full centre fuel tank could have triggered the explosion and issued urgent recommendations to the Federal Aviation Administration to act to prevent future such disasters.
But the NTSB stopped short of blaming the crash of the New York-to-Paris flight on mechanical failure, a bomb or a missile.

In answering the suits, TWA listed a number of possible causes for the explosion that were not the fault of the airline. It argued that TWA could not be held liable if the disaster was caused by parties for which the airline was not responsible.
For example, it stated that it could not be held responsible if the explosion was caused by a missile.

"In the alternative," the papers argued, if the explosion and resulting damages were "due to a meteorite or other 'Act of God' or were due to an unavoidable accident, sudden emergency, or other conditions or occurences" TWA would not be liable.
